In this video, you'll discover every way to use Claude Code, and learn how to build a real project with it — step by step, from installation to a finished pull request.
Let's start with a simple comparison.
A chat assistant can explain code and suggest changes. But you still copy the code, paste it into your files, run the tests, and fix the errors yourself.
Claude Code is different. It's an agentic coding tool. It reads your whole project, edits the files directly, runs commands and tests, and fixes problems — while you stay in control.
In short: a chat assistant gives advice. Claude Code does the work with you.
So, what exactly is Claude Code?
Claude Code is Anthropic's AI coding agent. It works right inside your project, wherever you write code.
It understands your codebase — searching and reading files to learn how everything fits together.
It takes action — editing files, running terminal commands, and working with git.
And it verifies its work — running tests and checks, and fixing what's broken.
At its core, Claude Code works in a loop.
First, it gathers context — reading the relevant files, and understanding your request.
Then it takes action — writing code, and editing files.
Next, it verifies — running tests, linters, or the app itself.
And it repeats, until the task is done and everything works.
You can use Claude Code in many places. Let's look at each one.
In the terminal, the command line interface gives you the full power of Claude Code, in any project.
In your IDE, extensions for VS Code and JetBrains show Claude's changes right next to your code.
The Claude desktop app gives you a visual interface for running Claude Code on your computer.
On the web and on mobile, Claude Code runs in secure cloud environments — so you can start tasks from anywhere.
In Slack, you can mention Claude in a conversation, and hand off coding tasks to it.
And in GitHub Actions and other automation, Claude Code can review pull requests and respond to issues automatically.
Before we build, here are four core concepts you'll use all the time.
CLAUDE dot M D is the project memory — a file with your commands, style rules, and conventions, that Claude reads automatically.
Plan mode lets Claude research and propose a plan, without changing anything yet.
Permissions control what Claude can do on its own, and when it should ask you first.
And checkpoints let you rewind — undoing Claude's changes and going back to an earlier point.
Now let's build a real project, step by step. Step one: install and start Claude Code.
Install it with a single command — using the native installer, or with npm.
Open your project folder in the terminal.
Type claude, to start a session.
And sign in with your Claude account, or with an API key. You're ready to go.
Step two: give Claude memory of your project. Run the slash init command, and Claude creates a CLAUDE dot M D file for you.
At the top, a short description of the project.
Next, the key commands — how to start the app, run the tests, and check the code style.
Then your code style — for example, TypeScript, React, and Tailwind.
And your rules — like always running tests before committing. Claude reads this file at the start of every session.
Step three: plan before you code. Press shift tab to switch between modes.
In plan mode, Claude can read and explore your code, but it doesn't change anything. It proposes a plan for you to review.
In the default mode, Claude asks for your permission before it edits files or runs commands.
In accept edits mode, Claude edits files automatically, while still asking before risky commands.
Start in plan mode for big features. Approve the plan, then let Claude build it.
Step four: build the feature. Describe what you want — for example: add a monthly budget limit, with a warning when spending goes over it.
Claude reads the relevant code, and finds where the change belongs.
It writes a step-by-step plan.
It edits the files — creating new components, and updating existing ones.
It runs the app and the tests, to check the result.
And it summarizes exactly what changed, so you can review it.
Step five: test and fix. Claude can run your tests, read the failures, and fix them — again and again.
Ask it to run the test suite, and make every test pass.
Claude runs the tests, studies each failure, and updates the code.
In this illustrative example, more tests pass with every round, until the whole suite is green.
Just make sure the tests themselves check the right things — Claude should fix the code, not weaken the tests.
Step six: review the changes. You stay in charge of your code.
Review the diff — in your IDE, or with git — to see every line that changed.
Ask questions. Claude can explain why it made each decision.
If you don't like a direction, rewind. Press escape twice, or use slash rewind, to go back to a checkpoint.
And when you're happy, approve the changes, and move on.
Step seven: commit and open a pull request. Just describe what you want in plain words.
Claude writes a clear commit message, based on the changes.
It pushes your branch to the remote repository.
And it opens a pull request, with a summary of what changed and why.
Your teammates can review it — and Claude can even help respond to their comments.
Step eight: extend Claude Code with powerful features.
Subagents are specialized helpers — like a code reviewer, or a test writer — each with its own focus.
Skills package know-how that Claude loads automatically, when a task needs it.
Hooks run your own commands automatically — like formatting every file Claude edits.
And MCP servers connect Claude Code to outside tools, like your issue tracker, databases, or design files. You can bundle all of these as plugins, and share them with your team.
Step nine: master the slash commands. Here are some of the most useful ones.
Slash init creates your CLAUDE dot M D. Slash clear starts a fresh conversation. And slash compact summarizes a long conversation, to free up space.
Slash model switches the Claude model. Slash rewind goes back to a checkpoint. And slash mcp manages your connected servers.
Slash agents manages your subagents, and slash permissions controls what Claude is allowed to do. Type a slash anytime, to see the full list.
Here are six best practices for working with Claude Code.
One: give clear, specific instructions — with file names, examples, and the result you expect.
Two: keep CLAUDE dot M D up to date, with your commands and rules.
Three: plan first, for big or risky changes.
Four: work in small steps, and commit often.
Five: always review the changes before you merge.
And six: use clear and compact, to keep each conversation focused.
Let's recap in one line: plan, build, ship.
Claude Code reads your code, makes changes, runs the tests, and opens the pull request — with you in control at every step.
